campbell-diagram.summary: Follow how vibration frequencies and amplitudes change as a shaft speeds up.
campbell-diagram.useWhen: Compare bearing run-ups, track harmonics tied to shaft rotation, or find speeds where vibration strengthens at a particular frequency.
campbell-diagram.data: Supply at least two nonnegative frequencies in Hz in strictly increasing order. Each run needs a unique id, a label, at least two nonnegative shaft speeds in RPM in strictly increasing order, and one spectrum of finite amplitudes per speed. The amplitude at speed index i and frequency index j is levelsDb[i][j].
campbell-diagram.reading: The heatmap shows shaft speed in RPM along the horizontal axis and vibration frequency in Hz along the vertical axis. Both bearing runs share the shaft speed, frequency, and relative amplitude scales. Areas outside the selected run’s measured speed range are blank. Select a shaft speed to inspect its complete spectrum.
notes: The measured example compares two University of Ottawa run-ups, a healthy bearing (H-A-1) and a bearing with an inner-race fault (I-A-1). The healthy run spans 862–1,420 RPM and the fault run spans 759–1,638 RPM.

Each run supplies 40 nonoverlapping 250 ms windows of 200 kHz accelerometer data. Each window is demeaned and Hann tapered before computing the FFT. The chart shows 100 frequency bins from 4 to 400 Hz. Speed is estimated from encoder pulse timing within each window.

The strongest amplitude across both runs and the displayed frequency band is the common 0 dB reference. For an amplitude spectrum, use 20 × log₁₀(amplitude / reference amplitude) and apply the same floor across runs.

The diagonal lines mark shaft orders. Order n occurs at n × RPM / 60 Hz. A ridge that follows an order tracks shaft rotation. A ridge that remains at the same frequency as speed changes can indicate a structural mode.
The heatmap interpolates between sample centers. The readout and spectrum show original bin values. Keep the windowing, frequency bins, and amplitude reference consistent when comparing runs.

mode-shapes.summary: See how a cantilever beam bends in each of its first four natural modes.
mode-shapes.useWhen: Compare bending patterns, locate vibration nodes, or connect a natural frequency to the shape of the corresponding motion.
mode-shapes.data: Supply a uniform rectangular beam with length, width, and thickness in metres, Young’s modulus in pascals, and density in kilograms per cubic metre. All values must be positive and finite. The example computes Euler–Bernoulli modes for a 600 × 30 × 3 mm steel strip with a modulus of 200 GPa and a density of 7,850 kg/m³.
mode-shapes.reading: Choose mode 1–4 to see its calculated natural frequency in Hz. The horizontal axis shows normalized span x/L, from 0 at the clamp to 1 at the free tip. The vertical axis shows normalized transverse deflection u/A₀ on a fixed scale shared by all four modes.
notes: The model computes free, undamped bending in the thickness direction. The clamp holds both displacement and slope at zero. The free end has zero bending moment and shear force.

The displayed deflection is u/A₀ = (s/100) cos(θ) φₙ(x)/φₙ(L). Here s is the deformation scale from 25% to 150%, θ is the phase, φₙ is the mode shape, and A₀ is an arbitrary reference tip amplitude at 100% scale.
Dashed curves mark the phase limits at 0° and 180° for the selected deformation scale. Hollow circles mark interior nodes, which stay at zero transverse deflection throughout the cycle.

Set the phase to 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270° for quarter-cycle snapshots. Playback shows one cycle in about 2.4 seconds for every mode. The modeled oscillation period in seconds is the reciprocal of the displayed natural frequency in Hz.
The example predicts frequencies of 6.79, 42.58, 119.23, and 233.65 Hz. The model assumes a slender beam with small deflections and an ideal clamp.
For this rectangular section, width cancels out of the ratio of bending stiffness to mass per unit length. Increasing thickness raises the natural frequencies, and increasing length lowers them.

shaft-orbit.summary: Follow the motion of a rotating shaft in two perpendicular probe signals.
shaft-orbit.useWhen: Compare the shape of an orbit across test runs, or check which part of each probe waveform produces a loop or turn in the path.
shaft-orbit.data: Give each run a unique ID, a label, a positive sample rate in Hz, and equal-length X and Y arrays of finite displacement values in µm. Both channels must share a sampling clock. Supply at least two strictly increasing, zero-based integer trigger indices inside the arrays. Each trigger marks the same shaft angle one revolution apart.
shaft-orbit.reading: Select a run and a revolution, then move the phase control. In the orbit, X displacement is horizontal and Y displacement is vertical. Both axes use equal physical scales in µm and the same limits across runs. The paired waveforms show X as a solid line and Y as a dashed line on the same time grid, in milliseconds from the trigger.
notes: The three simulated runs span 12 revolutions at 1,800 RPM (30 Hz), sampled at 5,760 Hz. The first shows a 30 Hz ellipse. The other two add a 60 Hz second harmonic (2×) or a 13.8 Hz subsynchronous component (0.46×). That lower-frequency component changes the orbit between turns.
Each simulated channel is centered by subtracting its mean over the 12 complete turns.

The solid navy orbit shows the selected revolution and dashed orbits show neighboring turns. The arrow points in the direction of motion as time advances. The open diamond marks the once-per-revolution trigger, and the hollow circle shows the point linked to both waveforms.

At 0°, the selected point sits on the first trigger in the selected turn. At 360°, it reaches the next trigger. Between triggers, the chart assumes constant speed and linearly interpolates between adjacent probe samples.

The reported RPM is 60 times the sample rate divided by the number of samples between adjacent triggers. Keep the probe orientation and sign conventions consistent across runs to compare orbit shape and direction.

frequency-response.summary: Inspect one complex frequency response as Bode magnitude, Bode phase, and a Nyquist curve.
frequency-response.useWhen: Compare controller gains, locate resonant peaks, or relate the phase and magnitude at a frequency to the loop’s position in the complex plane.
frequency-response.data: Supply one or more responses, each with a unique ID and a label. Provide at least two positive, strictly increasing frequencies in Hz. The real and imaginary arrays must have the same length as the frequency array, with a finite, nonzero complex magnitude at every sample.
frequency-response.reading: Choose a loop gain and select a frequency in a panel or with the Frequency control. Open circles identify the same sample in all three panels. The framed Bode panels align their logarithmic frequency ticks in Hz, with horizontal reference guides at 0 dB for magnitude and −180° for phase.
notes: The simulated loop combines a 28 Hz second-order elastic mode with damping ratio 0.14 and a first-order lag with a 45 Hz corner frequency. The example plots the modeled open-loop response at 301 sampled frequencies from 0.6 to 200 Hz for gains of 0.48 and 0.84.

The chart takes magnitude in decibels as 20 × log₁₀ of the complex modulus and phase as the signed angle in degrees. Phase unwrapping assumes the true phase changes by less than 180° between adjacent samples.

The white Nyquist panel uses equal scales for the horizontal real axis and the vertical imaginary axis. The solid curve joins the positive-frequency samples. For real-coefficient systems, the dashed negative-frequency branch is their complex conjugate reflected across the real axis.

The cross at (−1, 0) marks where 1 + L equals zero under unity negative feedback. Near 33.7 Hz the modeled nominal response crosses the real axis at about −0.68 and the higher-gain response crosses at about −1.20. The chart covers the sampled frequency band. A stability analysis needs the full Nyquist contour and the count of open-loop poles in the right half-plane.

coherence-phase.summary: Read magnitude-squared coherence and signed cross-phase at the same frequency.
coherence-phase.useWhen: Check which frequency components two sensors share and whether their relative phase is consistent over a test run.
coherence-phase.data: Supply spectral estimates from synchronized sensor recordings. For each run, provide a unique ID and label, at least two nonnegative frequencies in Hz in strictly increasing order, and aligned arrays of finite coherence and phase values. Coherence ranges from 0 to 1. Wrap phase to the −180° to 180° interval.
coherence-phase.reading: Choose a Recording, then select a frequency in either panel or with the Frequency control. A shared cursor identifies the same bin in the coherence and phase panels. Frequency band can restrict the view to the lower quarter of the range when that interval contains at least two bins.
notes: The example compares the first baseline and drive-end unbalance recordings at a nominal 30 Hz shaft speed (1,800 RPM) on the same Universidade de São Paulo rig. The source files are Normal_30Hz_001.lvm and Desbalanc1_30Hz_001.lvm. The unbalance recording lists an added 18.13 g mass at 0°.

Channel X is horizontal acceleration at the drive-end bearing and channel Y is horizontal acceleration at the non-drive-end bearing. Each six-second record contains 36,000 synchronized samples per channel at 6,000 Hz.

The displayed estimates use 34 Welch segments with per-segment mean removal, a 2,048-sample periodic Hann window, and 1,024 samples of overlap. The 512 displayed frequency bins span about 2.93–1,500 Hz with 2.93 Hz spacing. The preview starts on the bin nearest the nominal shaft speed, at 29.30 Hz.

Estimate the auto-spectra Pxx and Pyy and cross-spectrum Pxy with the same Welch window, segment length, overlap, and sampling rate. Magnitude-squared coherence is |Pxy|²/(Pxx Pyy). Values near 1 indicate a consistent linear association at that frequency.

The phase convention is Y relative to X. Phase is arg(Pxy), where the Welch cross-spectrum averages segment products conj(X)Y. Swapping X and Y reverses the phase sign. A pure delay τ from X to Y gives phase −360° × frequency × τ modulo 360°, with time in seconds.

Coherence threshold starts at 0.60 and controls the phase display. Phase has gaps at bins below the selected cutoff and at jumps across the ±180° wrap. Interpreting phase or choosing a statistical threshold requires knowledge of the sensor setup and the spectral estimates.

wavelet-scalogram.summary: Locate short vibration events and changing frequencies, then inspect the waveform at the same time.
wavelet-scalogram.useWhen: Analyze a signal whose frequency content changes over time, such as during a machine run-up or a short vibration burst.
wavelet-scalogram.data: Supply strictly increasing times in seconds, strictly increasing positive frequencies in Hz, and a matrix of finite relative power values in dB. Index the matrix as powerDb[frequencyIndex][timeIndex]. Provide the matching waveform with startSeconds, a positive sampleRateHz, a unit label, and uniformly sampled finite values.
wavelet-scalogram.reading: The scalogram plots time horizontally and frequency on a logarithmic vertical axis. The colorbar shows wavelet power relative to the peak. Select a time and frequency in the map or with the controls. Use Waveform window to inspect the linked signal at 1 ms, 10 ms, 50 ms, 250 ms, or 1 s. The readout gives the waveform value of the sample nearest the selected time.
notes: The lower pane shows 512,000 original 200 kHz Channel_1 samples from 3.500000 to 6.059995 s of the University of Ottawa I-A-1 inner-race fault run-up. The sample values retain their recorded scale. The pane uses channel units because the source leaves the stored amplitude unit unspecified.

When a waveform window contains more samples than horizontal pixels, the trace keeps each display bin’s minimum and maximum in chronological order. Only detailed previews request the original waveform. If it is unavailable, the lower pane is labeled as the processed 12.5 kHz waveform in segment RMS units.

At the initial scalogram time of 4.606 s, the original sample reads approximately 0.133943 channel units. The largest sample in the original excerpt is approximately 0.741982 channel units at 5.885025 s.

The scalogram uses a separate processed signal. The full recording is low-pass filtered with a Kaiser window (β = 5) and resampled to 12.5 kHz before extracting 3.500–6.060 s. The excerpt is demeaned and scaled by its root-mean-square amplitude before the transform.

The transform uses zero-padded convolution with a sampled unit-energy complex Morlet wavelet (ω₀ = 6). The map contains 100 log-spaced equivalent Fourier frequencies from 30 to 3,000 Hz and 640 four-millisecond time bins. Each cell retains the maximum wavelet power in its time bin.

For transform coefficients W, compute power P = |W|² and report 10 × log₁₀(P/Pₘₐₓ). The strongest retained cell in this map sets 0 dB, and the display floor is −60 dB. Keep the wavelet, scaling, and reference consistent when comparing levels.

The cone-of-influence boundaries mark where finite-record edges can affect the estimates. coiEdgeSeconds supplies one inward time margin per frequency row, set to √2 times the Morlet scale in this example. Lower-frequency wavelets extend farther in time.

bearing-envelope.summary: Select a carrier band and inspect the corresponding vibration envelope in shaft orders.
bearing-envelope.useWhen: Explore repeated amplitude modulation in accelerometer recordings, or compare how different carrier bands reveal different repetition rates as a shaft speeds up.
bearing-envelope.data: Supply shared, strictly increasing frequency bins in Hz and shaft-order bins. Define each band with a unique id, a label, and its lower and upper limits in Hz. Each recording supplies a broadbandDb array aligned to frequencyHz and one envelope array aligned to orders per band id. Supply finite relative levels in dB with a common reference for each panel across recordings and bands.
bearing-envelope.reading: Choose a bearing recording and a carrier band. The broadband panel highlights that band in Hz and the envelope panel shows modulation in cycles per shaft revolution. Select an order to read its level. Relative dB scales stay fixed while you compare bands and recordings.
notes: The University of Ottawa example compares the healthy H-A-1 and inner-race fault I-A-1 run-ups. Channel_1 acceleration is low-pass filtered with a Kaiser window (β = 5) and resampled from 200 kHz to 20 kHz. Each analysis uses 60 measured shaft turns starting at the first 2 V rising crossing of the Channel_2 encoder signal after 3.000 s.

The broadband panel estimates power spectral density with Welch averaging, using 1,024-sample periodic Hann windows, 512 samples of overlap, and removal of each segment mean. It shows 409 positive bins from about 19.53 to 7,988.28 Hz. Carrier bands are 800–1,600, 1,600–3,200, and 3,200–6,400 Hz.

For each carrier band, apply a forward–reverse Butterworth band-pass filter with order parameter 4 and take the magnitude of the Hilbert analytic signal. A forward–reverse 450 Hz low-pass filter with order parameter 8 limits the envelope before interpolation onto every eighth encoder pulse, giving 128 samples per shaft revolution.

The envelope order spectrum uses the demeaned signal with a periodic Hann window and amplitude correction for window gain. The display contains 900 positive bins from 1/60 to 15 shaft orders. The broadband level is 10 × log₁₀ of the ratio to the shared peak power spectral density. The envelope level is 20 × log₁₀ of the ratio to the shared peak amplitude across runs and bands. Both displays have a −65 dB floor.

The ER16K bearing geometry gives expected ball-pass references at 3.57 orders for the outer race (BPFO) and 5.43 orders for the inner race (BPFI), with the second BPFI harmonic at 10.86 orders. The example opens on the inner-race recording in the 3,200–6,400 Hz carrier band at 5.45 orders. These guides are geometric predictions, and interpretation depends on the operating conditions, slip, and sensor response.

eye-diagram.summary: Overlay symbol intervals to compare voltage margin, crossing jitter, and overshoot in a binary signal.
eye-diagram.useWhen: Explore where to sample an NRZ signal or compare how channel impairments affect the eye opening.
eye-diagram.data: Supply strictly increasing time samples in unit intervals (UI), spanning at least 0 to 1 UI, and a positive symbol rate in baud. Each run supplies a unique id, a label, nominal low and high voltage levels in mV, and folded traces whose voltages align to timeUi. For each trace, previousBit labels the bit before 0 UI and bit labels the bit in the central interval.
eye-diagram.reading: Choose a Channel and use Sampling phase to move the sampling line through the central symbol interval. The eye height updates at the selected phase, which starts at 0.5 UI. The crossing bracket spans the fifth to 95th percentiles of crossing times near the leading symbol boundary.
notes: Each channel simulates one full 127-symbol PRBS7 period at 1 Gbaud with nominal levels of −400 and 400 mV. The 127 folds span −0.5 to 1.5 UI at 64 samples per UI against an ideal clock. At this symbol rate, 1 UI is 1,000 ps.

The reference channel uses a critically damped second-order response. The impaired channel has lower damping, with 24% of the response delayed by 0.58 UI, larger timing offsets, and more voltage noise. Both channels use periodic and seeded random timing offsets.

At the selected phase the chart linearly interpolates each trace between sampled voltages. Eye height is the fifth percentile of high-bit voltages minus the 95th percentile of low-bit voltages. A negative height means the two percentile bounds overlap.

Crossing jitter uses traces with a bit change. For each trace, use the same-direction crossing of the nominal rail midpoint closest to 0 UI within ±0.35 UI, found by linear interpolation. Include only traces with a crossing in that window. RMS jitter is the population root mean square of those crossing times after subtracting their mean, converted to picoseconds using the symbol rate.
Overshoot reports the greatest excursion above the high rail or below the low rail across the folded traces, as a percentage of the nominal full swing. The lower-rail excursion is undershoot.
At 0.5 UI the reference and impaired eye heights are about 795 and 364 mV, respectively. The simulations give about 3.5 and 39.6 ps RMS crossing jitter and 0.49% and 8.51% overshoot.

allan-deviation.summary: Compare the stability of a measured quantity across different averaging times.
allan-deviation.useWhen: Inspect clock frequency or inertial-sensor noise over short and long averaging intervals.
allan-deviation.data: Supply the name of the measured quantity and its unit if applicable. Give each curve a unique ID, a label, and points ordered by strictly increasing averaging time. Each point needs a positive finite tauSeconds and deviation for the logarithmic axes. Add pairs when the number of contributing overlapping terms is available.
allan-deviation.reading: The horizontal axis is averaging time τ in seconds and the vertical axis is Allan deviation in the quantity’s units. Both axes are logarithmic. Choose a Recording, then use Averaging time or the plot to read deviation and the overlapping pair count when supplied. Lower deviation indicates more stable averages at that timescale.
notes: The example uses 44,002 synchronized phase samples, one second apart, from the NIST optical-clock and 10 GHz microwave comparison. Convert recorded phase φ in radians to time error x = φ/(2πν), using the experiment’s 259 THz optical reference and 10 GHz microwave reference. Convert the recorded microwave values from milliradians first.

The difference curve uses the sample-by-sample microwave time error minus optical time error. It describes the paired recordings, both of which compare two devices. Nakamura et al. report their separate optical-to-microwave transfer measurement in the paper.

Overlapping Allan deviation compares adjacent averages of duration τ. Start successive pairs one sample apart. For this one-second time-error data, τ = m seconds and each contributing value is (x[i + 2m] − 2x[i + m] + x[i])/τ. The deviation is the square root of one half the mean square of the N − 2m terms. The example spans 1–10,000 s.

At τ = 100 s the optical and microwave deviations are about 2.86 × 10⁻¹⁷ and 2.87 × 10⁻¹⁷. Their matched-record difference has deviation 3.45 × 10⁻¹⁸. Each estimate uses 43,802 overlapping terms, which share input samples. Confidence intervals depend on the effective degrees of freedom, the noise process, and the averaging factor.

Show reference slopes adds ideal power-law guides on the log–log plot. White frequency modulation (FM) has slope −½, flicker FM has slope 0, and random-walk FM has slope +½. Compare the surrounding points and the record length when interpreting a measured slope.

phase-plane.summary: Follow position and velocity together, with the selected state linked to its time in the trajectory.
phase-plane.useWhen: Inspect how an oscillator approaches equilibrium, compare trajectories under different damping, or examine the direction of motion in state space.
phase-plane.data: Supply labels and units for the position and velocity axes. Give each trajectory a unique ID, a label, and samples with strictly increasing timeSeconds and finite position and velocity values. For a continuous rotation, supply an unwrapped angular position coordinate.
phase-plane.reading: Choose a Trajectory and move the Time control or select a point on the linked position history. The main plot shows position horizontally and velocity vertically, with an arrow pointing in the direction of increasing time. The markers identify the same recorded state in both views.
notes: The example uses three recordings of the same 0.607 m pendulum from the Damped Pendulum Dataset. The damping setups are air only, a small paper baffle, and a large paper baffle. The PASCO PS-3220 recordings report angle in radians and angular velocity in radians per second at 100 Hz.

The excerpts use trials len5_cond1_2, len5_cond2_2, and len5_cond3_1. Time starts at the last recorded zero-velocity sample before the sustained inward swing. Starting angles are 0.553, 0.603, and 0.559 rad. The chart retains every fourth sample through 16 s, for 401 displayed samples per trajectory at 25 Hz.
For an undriven pendulum, the hanging state at zero angle and zero angular velocity is an equilibrium. With dissipation, the measured loops contract as the motion approaches that state.

The copyable oscillator example supplies a model for the direction field. Pass acceleration(position, velocity) to draw the rate vector (velocity, acceleration) at each state. Use consistent units, with velocity equal to position units per second and acceleration equal to velocity units per second. Show direction field toggles the model arrows when valid acceleration values are available.

xrd-peak-tracker.summary: Inspect a diffraction peak fit and follow its center, width, and height across temperatures.
xrd-peak-tracker.useWhen: Compare how an observed feature shifts, broadens, or changes height in temperature-resolved diffraction scans.
xrd-peak-tracker.data: Supply a shared, strictly increasing angleDeg axis in degrees 2θ. Provide scans in increasing temperature order in kelvin, with one finite intensity value per angle. Give each peak a unique ID, a label, a fixed window in degrees 2θ, and one fit per scan in the same order. Use null when a fit is unavailable.
xrd-peak-tracker.reading: Choose a Peak and move the Temperature control. In the DyNiC₂ waterfall, you can also select a measured point inside a fitted angle window to inspect that scan’s fit. The profile shows measured sample markers, a fitted curve over the fixed window, and its linear background. The bracket marks the full width at half maximum (FWHM). Three aligned temperature plots follow the fitted center, FWHM, and peak height above background.
notes: The example uses 16 measured DyNiC₂ synchrotron X-ray diffraction scans from 10.91 to 294.11 K. The scans share 163 samples from about 5.002 to 5.500° 2θ. The fixed windows are 5.157–5.247°, 5.252–5.322°, and 5.324–5.407° and identify observed features by angle.

Bounded, unweighted least squares fits a pseudo-Voigt peak, a Gaussian–Lorentzian mixture with a shared center and width, plus a linear background. The background intercept is defined at the fitted center. Height is the fitted peak contribution above that background, in arbitrary intensity units (a.u.). FWHM measures the separation of the points at half that height above the local background.

The fit tries starting Lorentzian fractions of 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9. Among converged solutions with finite parameters and center, width, and height away from their bounds, it selects the smallest sum of squared intensity residuals. The example retains all 48 fits. An unavailable fit appears as a gap in the temperature trends.

stress-strain-comparison.useWhen: Compare recorded tensile responses across heat treatments or inspect how an elastic fit defines an offset proof stress.
stress-strain-comparison.data: Give each curve a unique ID, a label, and finite engineering stress in MPa at strictly increasing engineering strain. Supply strain as a fraction, so 0.002 represents 0.2%. Provide the elastic-fit strain bounds, slope in MPa, and stress intercept in MPa. Use optional elongationAfterFracture for the specimen result as a fraction, so 0.053 represents 5.3%. A zero-based fractureIndex ends the curve at a documented break point.
stress-strain-comparison.reading: Choose a Condition. The main panel overlays the recorded curves. The detail panel shows the selected curve at low strain, its fitted elastic line, and the parallel line shifted by 0.2% strain. The proof-stress marker sits where the offset line intersects the curve. When supplied, “Elongation after fracture, A” gives the reported result for the selected specimen.
notes: The example compares measured EN AW-2618A tensile curves for the T61 reference (ABR5RTzl1) and after 15,000 h of additional ageing at 160 °C (ABR10RTzl1) or 190 °C (ABR8RTzl1). Each test used a DIN 50125 B6 × 30 specimen at 20 °C and a nominal strain rate of 0.0001 s⁻¹ under ISO 6892-1.

Engineering strain uses the original gauge length and engineering stress divides force by the original cross-sectional area. The figure retains measured points at successive new highs in strain, then selects points by strain bin while preserving the proof-stress bracket, tensile maximum, and last retained point.

The modulus estimate E is the slope of the elastic fit Eε + b. The example uses ordinary least squares on 0.05–0.15% strain for all three curves. The offset line is E(ε − 0.002) + b. The chart interpolates the first crossing of that line after the fit interval where the curve moves from above to below it.

The calculated 0.2% proof stresses are about 363, 283, and 249 MPa for T61, 160 °C ageing, and 190 °C ageing, respectively. The corresponding recorded tensile maxima are 428.7, 362.0, and 342.8 MPa. Each plotted endpoint represents the last retained stress–strain sample.

Elongation after fracture A is the reported permanent elongation relative to the original gauge length. The source workbook’s Tensiletest overview gives 5.3% for ABR5RTzl1, 8.2% for ABR10RTzl1, and 7.9% for ABR8RTzl1.

The example plots 22 measured tests from the FABEST v4 workbook (CC BY 4.0). Setups 37 and 35 used hollow, unnotched steel specimens under constant-amplitude axial tension–compression at R = −1. The vertical axis shows nominal stress amplitude on the net section.

crack-growth.data: Give each series a unique ID and at least three points ordered by increasing or equal deltaK. Both deltaK in MPa√m and rateMmPerCycle in mm/cycle must be finite and positive. Supply stressRatio when available. Optional fitRange sets the initial ΔK bounds and needs at least three points spanning two distinct ΔK values. Otherwise the chart starts with the full series.
crack-growth.reading: Both axes are logarithmic. The horizontal axis is stress-intensity factor range ΔK, in MPa√m. The vertical axis is crack advance per cycle da/dN, in mm/cycle. Use Series to switch curves when multiple are available. Click a marker or use Measurement to read its values. Set Fit from and Fit through to change which points are included in the fit. Filled markers are included and open markers are outside the fit interval.
notes: In the Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, m is the slope of log₁₀(da/dN) against log₁₀(ΔK) and log₁₀(C) is the intercept. The chart estimates both by ordinary least squares on the selected points and reports R² in log space with the count of those points.
C uses units of (mm/cycle)/(MPa√m)ᵐ. Compare coefficients after matching the units and accounting for the specimen, loading conditions, and fitted interval.
Select the approximately linear part of the log–log curve for a Paris-law fit. The line spans the selected observations. Threshold and rapid fracture regions may follow different relationships.

The example compares S460, S690, and S960 compact-tension curves from Seitl et al. The specimens had the same effective width (50 mm) and thickness (10 mm) and were tested at 22 ± 1 °C in opening mode (mode I), with a force ratio of R = 0.1. The study estimated crack length from the compliance of clip-gauge measurements of crack mouth opening displacement (CMOD).

The example groups points by steel grade and uses the positive ΔK and da/dN pairs from the workbook’s selected CMOD columns. The plotted values retain their published units. Each grade starts with the common 10–20 MPa√m fit interval. The displayed coefficients depend on the measurements that fall inside that interval.

binary-phase-diagram.summary: Explore how the equilibrium phases of a two-component material change with composition and temperature.
binary-phase-diagram.useWhen: Read liquidus, solidus, and solvus boundaries, follow a fixed-composition cooling path, and calculate fractions in a two-phase field.
binary-phase-diagram.data: Provide two distinct component names, the composition unit (at. % or wt. % of the second component), a temperature domain in °C, a eutectic temperature and three compositions, and six boundary branches. Each branch needs at least two samples with composition from 0 to 100 and strictly increasing temperatures within the display domain. On each side, join the liquidus and solidus at the corresponding pure-component melting point. Each solvus spans the display minimum to the eutectic. Match every branch at the eutectic temperature to its corresponding eutectic composition.
binary-phase-diagram.reading: The horizontal axis gives the overall percentage of the second component and the vertical axis gives temperature. Click or drag the point on the figure, or use Composition and Temperature. Follow the vertical path to see which fields the alloy enters on cooling. In a two-phase field, the ends of the horizontal tie line show the compositions of the two phases. Use Go to eutectic to select the exact invariant temperature and liquid composition.
notes: The liquidus separates fully liquid material from liquid plus solid. The solidus marks the limit of fully solid material. A solvus marks the composition limit of a solid solution.

For a bulk composition x₀ between tie-line endpoints xₗ and xᵣ, the fraction of the left phase is (xᵣ − x₀)/(xᵣ − xₗ) and the fraction of the right phase is (x₀ − xₗ)/(xᵣ − xₗ). With atomic percent these are mole fractions on an atom basis. With weight percent they are mass fractions.

Between the solid endpoints of the invariant eutectic line, three equilibrium phase compositions are fixed. Bulk composition and temperature provide too little information to determine three phase fractions. The diagram represents equilibrium at the specified pressure. Rates of solidification and diffusion require a kinetic model.

The Ag–Cu example uses the Moon et al. thermodynamic assessment from Hallstedt’s SGTE collection. ORCHID calculated the equilibrium boundaries with pycalphad 0.11.2 at 1 atm. The figure converts kelvin to °C and Cu mole fraction to atomic percent. Tie-line endpoints are linearly interpolated from the published boundary samples.

The calculated eutectic is at 779.13 °C. The Ag-rich solid, liquid, and Cu-rich solid compositions there are 13.274, 40.254, and 95.460 at. % Cu. The separate NIST Ag–Cu calculation reports a liquid eutectic composition of 28.41 wt. % Cu using its own assessment.
At 20 at. % Cu and 850 °C, the Ag-rich solid contains about 9.08 at. % Cu and the liquid about 21.62 at. % Cu. The lever rule gives about 87.1% liquid on a mole basis.

Register both surfaces in one physical coordinate frame before passing the data. Optionally set sectionAxis, a positive colorLimitMm, and a nonnegative toleranceMm.
cad-scan-deviation.reading: Drag the 3D view or use Rotate left and Rotate right. With focus on the 3D view, press Up or Down to change the tilt. Select a measured point in either view to inspect its signed deviation and bring the section through that point. With focus on the section, press Left or Right to select a nearby measured point. Use Show nominal surface to control the 3D reference overlay. Move Section position to intersect the nominal mesh with a plane and see nearby scan points projected onto it. Use Tolerance (mm) to set the symmetric deviation band and Outside tolerance only to filter the measured points.
notes: The distance magnitude is the Euclidean distance to the nearest point on the nominal surface. The sign follows the orientation of the nearest reference face. A positive deviation is on the normal-facing side. A negative deviation is on the opposite side. Use consistent reference normals when computing signed distances.

The color bar gives signed deviations in millimeters. Blue marks negative deviations and red marks positive deviations. Values beyond the endpoints use the endpoint colors and keep their numerical deviation. Tolerance is applied to the absolute deviation before rounding the readout. The section projects samples from a slab around the plane and retains their supplied 3D deviations.

The viewer uses the supplied alignment and point-to-surface distances. Document the frame, registration method, and reference orientation alongside your data. The tolerance control applies a band to the supplied points. A part-level conformance decision also depends on its tolerance specification, scan coverage, and measurement uncertainty.

The example compares measured Part 4 from the NIST Overhang Part X4 study with its nominal 9 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm CAD geometry. The part was printed in nickel superalloy 625 with a 45° overhang and a horizontal cylindrical cutout. NIST measured the part with X-ray CT at 11.95 µm isotropic voxel pitch and published the cleaned surface mesh.

To sample the measured mesh, the example takes vertices from every 32nd triangle and keeps a representative nearest the center of each occupied 0.32 mm bin. Distances for the resulting 3,601 locations use all 2,904 triangles of the original nominal mesh. The viewer uses a lighter 1,464-triangle mesh to draw the nominal surface.

At the example’s ±0.10 mm tolerance, 1,269 of the 3,601 sampled locations are outside the band. The color bar spans ±0.60 mm. The initial point at about (1.063, 2.421, 3.453) mm lies inside the nominal bore with a positive deviation of 1.044 mm. Its color reaches the endpoint while the readout retains its value. cie-chromaticity.summary: Compare display gamuts and inspect sample chromaticities in two coordinate systems using the CIE 1931 standard observer.
cie-chromaticity.useWhen: Check which measured samples lie inside a target gamut, compare standardized or measured primaries, or quantify how much of one gamut a second gamut covers.
cie-chromaticity.data: Supply at least three spectral-locus samples in increasing wavelength order, each with a wavelength in nanometers and its CIE 1931 xy coordinates. Give each gamut a unique ID, a label, and at least three non-collinear primaries in xy. The chart uses their convex hull. An optional white point must lie within its gamut. Supply optional samples with unique IDs, labels, and CIE 1931 xy coordinates inside or on the visible chromaticity boundary. Use initialPoint and initialGamuts to set the starting probe and comparison.
cie-chromaticity.reading: Choose Reference gamut to set the target and Comparison gamut to compare it with another region. Click a sample marker or choose its label in Measured sample to inspect its coordinates and gamut membership. Marker shapes distinguish samples inside the reference gamut from those outside it. The sample stays selected when you switch gamuts, switch Coordinate space between CIE 1931 xy and CIE 1976 u′v′, or turn off Show sample markers. Choose Free probe or click an unmarked position within the visible boundary to inspect a position independently. With the plot focused, use the arrow keys to move the free probe by 0.005 in the active coordinates, or hold Shift to move by 0.025.
notes: The spectral locus is the curved boundary of monochromatic stimuli for the CIE 1931 2° standard observer. The straight line of purples joins its endpoints and describes mixtures of long- and short-wavelength light.
For CIE 1976 u′v′, let D = 3 − 2x + 12y. Then u′ = 4x/D and v′ = 9y/D. Switching spaces changes the plotted coordinates of the same chromaticity.

Coverage is the area common to both gamut polygons divided by the area of the reference polygon in the selected coordinate space. The comparison percentage uses the comparison polygon as the denominator. Switching coordinate spaces can change both percentages. This is a two-dimensional chromaticity area. Assessing color volume also requires a brightness or lightness dimension.
Sample containment counts individual points inside each gamut, including points on its boundary. The counts depend on the supplied samples and stay the same across coordinate spaces.

The example uses 471 published CIE locus samples from 360 to 830 nm in 1 nm steps. The three standardized gamuts are sRGB, Display P3, and Rec. 2020 (ITU-R BT.2020). Their D65 white point is (0.3127, 0.3290) in xy and approximately (0.19783, 0.46832) in u′v′.

The 99 CIE color evaluation samples use published spectral radiance factors. Their xy coordinates are calculated by combining those spectra with illuminant D65 and the CIE 1931 2° color-matching functions at 1 nm steps from 380 to 780 nm, then normalizing the resulting XYZ values.

With sRGB as the reference and Display P3 as the comparison, 93 of the 99 samples lie inside sRGB and all 99 lie inside Display P3. Select CES 53 · Plastic to inspect a sample at approximately (0.2348, 0.4318) in xy that lies outside sRGB and inside Display P3.

Set Display P3 as Reference gamut and sRGB as Comparison gamut to see about 73.72% coverage in xy and 79.64% in u′v′. With the two gamuts reversed, Display P3 covers 100% of sRGB in both coordinate spaces. With Display P3 as the reference and Rec. 2020 as the comparison, coverage rounds to 99.98% in both spaces.
The diagram’s background uses illustrative sRGB colors. Use the locus, gamut boundaries, and coordinate readout for comparison.

hyperspectral-cube.summary: Inspect a stack of spectral images and compare the spectrum of one pixel with a region average.
hyperspectral-cube.useWhen: Explore which wavelengths distinguish spatial features in imaging spectroscopy data, or compare spectral variation within a region.
hyperspectral-cube.data: Supply positive integer dimensions, strictly increasing positive wavelengths in nanometers, and exactly width × height × band count values. Store each band as a complete image, with the column changing fastest. The flat index is b × width × height + y × width + x. Use noDataValue for a raw-value sentinel and excludedBands for zero-based band indices. Keep at least two bands available for inspection.
hyperspectral-cube.reading: Under Image mode, choose Single band for a grayscale image or RGB composite to assign wavelengths with Red band, Green band, and Blue band. Click or tap the image to inspect one pixel, or drag a rectangle to read a region spectrum. With the image focused, use arrow keys to pick a pixel or hold Shift to extend the region from its anchor. Pick a wavelength on the spectrum or use Wavelength band to switch the image to that band. With the spectrum focused, Left and Right step between bands. Home and End jump to the first and last available bands.
notes: Each valid sample is displayed as raw × valueScale + valueOffset. Source column and Source row are columnOrigin + x × pixelStride and rowOrigin + y × pixelStride. The initialPixel indexes the local cube. Use zero-based band indices for initialBand and for rgbBands ordered red, green, blue. A common display range keeps the image contrast scale fixed across wavelengths and RGB channels.

The region spectrum plots the mean of valid pixels at each wavelength. Across adjacent bands with two or more valid pixels, the envelope extends one population standard deviation above and below the mean. A band’s valid count can vary because no-data pixels are excluded separately at each wavelength.

Excluded bands and bands with zero valid pixels break the spectrum. RGB composite colors reflect the chosen channel wavelengths and the display range. Assigning infrared bands produces a false-color image. Use the spectral readout for numerical comparison.

The measured example uses NASA/JPL AVIRIS data acquired over Cuprite, Nevada, on June 23, 1995. The published cube is radiative transfer ground calibrated (RTGC). A stored value of 20,000 represents 100% reflectance, so each integer step is 0.005 percentage point. The archive uses −32,767 for deleted samples.

The 108 × 84 crop starts at zero-based source column 161 and row 409 and keeps every third source pixel along each axis. It retains 126 original bands from 383.15 to 2508.20 nm in wavelength order, with denser sampling between 2050 and 2400 nm. Eight retained bands near the low-signal atmospheric water absorption regions around 1400 and 1900 nm are excluded from inspection.

The opening false-color composite assigns 2270.05, 2210.28, and 2090.47 nm to red, green, and blue, using a fixed 19–40% image display range. The starting pixel at source column 416 and row 526 has 29.12% reflectance at 2210.28 nm. The same pixel reads 34.085% at 2150.42 nm and 34.575% at 2260.10 nm.

Select source columns 404–416 and rows 511–526 to compare the starting pixel with its neighborhood. At 2210.28 nm the 30 sampled pixels give a mean of about 31.347% and a population standard deviation of 3.316 percentage points.

response-surface.summary: Explore a fitted response to two factors in linked 3D, contour, and cross-section views alongside measured trials.
response-surface.useWhen: Find factor combinations that produce a similar fitted response, compare observations with their fitted values, or hold one factor fixed to study the other.
response-surface.data: Supply axis labels and units, measured trials with unique IDs and finite x, y, and response values in physical units, and an evaluate(x, y) function that returns the fitted response. The chart uses the convex hull of the measured factor settings by default. To set an explicit supported domain, provide its boundary vertices in factor coordinates and include every observed setting. Use initialPosition and sectionAxis to set the starting probe and section.
response-surface.reading: Click or drag within the contour map to move the probe and its cross-section. With the map focused, use the arrow keys to move along the factor axes. Select a position on the 3D surface to inspect its fitted response. Drag the 3D view or use Rotate left and Rotate right. With the 3D view focused, Up and Down change its tilt. Click a trial or choose its ID from Trial to compare its measured and fitted responses. Use Fixed factor and Section position to adjust the section. Click the section or focus it and use Left and Right to move the probe. Home and End jump to the section endpoints.
notes: The mesh shows the fitted response. Points are individual observations. Each vertical segment joins an observation to the fit at the same factor settings. Residuals are observed minus fitted. Points at the same x and y can have different measured responses.

Each contour line connects points at one fitted response level. The filled bands show intervals in the same response units as the 3D surface. The map derives these levels from the triangles of the displayed mesh and leaves the area outside the factor domain blank.

The line through the probe on the contour map shows where the section fixes one factor and sweeps the other. Only trials at that fixed setting appear in the section. All three views stop at the factor-domain boundary. By default, that boundary is the convex hull of the measured settings. Predictions between measured settings depend on the chosen model.

The example uses eleven reported run means from Kim et al.’s central composite design, with temperatures of 40–100 °C and times of 5–60 minutes. For each run, the authors averaged five beads. Sphericity was calculated from microscope images as 100 times the minor diameter divided by the major diameter.

The fit is an unweighted quadratic regression on the eleven published run means at their tabulated physical factor settings. It has an in-sample RMSE of about 0.289 percentage points. The nine distinct settings form an octagonal factor domain.

At 70 °C and 32.5 min the fitted response is 98.297%. Select run-09, run-10, and run-11 individually to see measured sphericities of 98.0%, 98.2%, and 98.7% and residuals of −0.297, −0.097, and +0.403 percentage points.

pca-biplot.summary: Display measured specimens and variable directions in one principal component analysis (PCA) view.
pca-biplot.useWhen: Explore how measurements covary, which variables distinguish specimens, and where known product groups overlap.
pca-biplot.data: Supply at least three observations and two quantitative variables with enough independent variation to yield two components. Assign unique, nonblank IDs to variables and observations. Each observation needs a finite value for every variable in the same order. Add variable labels and optional units, and optional observation labels and groups.
pca-biplot.reading: Points represent specimens and arrows show variable directions. The axis labels report how much of the total standardized variance each component explains. Drag a rectangle to select points and inspect the linked specimen table. Select a variable and specimen to see the specimen’s signed projection along the arrow and compare the two-component estimate with the measured value.
notes: PCA centers each column and divides by its sample standard deviation. Constant columns have zero contribution. Group labels identify specimens on the plot and are excluded from the fit. Each component is oriented so its largest absolute coefficient is positive.

Score scaling assigns the full component scale to specimen points, loading scaling assigns it to variable arrows, and balanced scaling shares it equally. The first mode emphasizes distances between specimens in the retained components, while the second emphasizes relationships between variables. All three keep the fitted components and explained variance fixed.

Scores use the bottom and left axes. Loadings use the top and right axes, which share the score origin and have a different calibration. Multiply the signed projection in score coordinates by the arrow length in loading coordinates to get the standardized estimate from the first two components. The fitted mean and standard deviation convert that estimate back to the measurement’s original units.

The glass example uses all 214 UCI specimens. The nine measurements are dimensionless refractive index and the weight percentages of oxides corresponding to sodium, magnesium, aluminum, silicon, potassium, calcium, barium, and iron. pareto-frontier.summary: Compare three competing objectives and identify trials that set the best observed trade-offs.
pareto-frontier.useWhen: Find process runs that balance production rate, energy, and product performance, then check which remain eligible under a minimum or maximum requirement.
pareto-frontier.data: Supply exactly three objectives with labels, optional short labels and units, and a minimize or maximize direction for each. Give each trial a unique ID and three finite objective values in matching order. Add a label, trial group, or setup details if available.
pareto-frontier.reading: The 3D attainment boundary steps at target levels supported by eligible trials. The axis arrows indicate the preferred direction. Switch to Threshold section to see the attainable targets for the first two objectives at the selected third-objective requirement. Use the threshold to set a minimum for a maximized objective or a maximum for a minimized objective. Select a point or use Inspect trial to see its measurements and status.
notes: A trial dominates another when it is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in at least one. The chart recalculates dominance among the eligible trials when the threshold or trial group changes. Trials with equal objective values keep their own IDs and share the same status.

The staircase shows the boundary of targets met by at least one eligible trial. Its steps retain the observed objective values. Each area in the threshold section corresponds to targets that an eligible trial meets simultaneously.

The maize germ example uses the three active screw speeds in Table 1, measured in 10-minute steady-state intervals. Feed rate in kg/h is the reciprocal of specific pressing time in h/kg feed. Specific press energy stays in the reported kJ/kg feed. Feed oil removed is 100% minus the reported percentage of initial oil retained in the cake.

At 11, 16.5, and 22 rpm, the press removes 55%, 43%, and 34% of feed oil by that measure. All three trials are nondominated. At 16.5 rpm the press uses the least specific energy, 589 kJ/kg feed. Setting the minimum oil removed to 43% leaves two eligible trials.

The AISI 316L example uses 54 turning trials, split equally between dry and minimum-quantity lubrication (MQL). It computes nominal removal rate as V × f × aₚ in cm³/min and estimates specific cutting energy as Fz ÷ (3600 × f × aₚ) in kWh/dm³. V is cutting speed in m/min, f is feed in mm/rev, aₚ is the 0.5 mm depth of cut, and Fz is the measured tangential force in newtons. Surface roughness Ra is the measured finish criterion.

With all 54 turning trials eligible, runs 5, 17, 19, 45, and 47 are nondominated. Run 17 has a nominal removal rate of 20 cm³/min, an estimated specific cutting energy of 0.5563 kWh/dm³, and a measured Ra of 0.25 µm. Setting maximum Ra to 0.30 µm leaves seven eligible trials, of which two are nondominated.

spatial-defect-map.summary: Locate individual die failures and inspect connected clusters across wafers and batches.
spatial-defect-map.useWhen: Compare wafer-sort results, investigate the shape of failure clusters, or identify which locations were missing or untested.
spatial-defect-map.data: Supply wafer IDs, batch labels, a grid geometry, and die records with unique integer row and column pairs. Each site has a pass, fail, untested, or missing status. A failed die may reference a declared failure bin. Omit cells outside the recorded grid footprint. Specify pitch, coordinate unit, optional origin and row direction, and a radius and notch where measured or declared.
spatial-defect-map.reading: Choose a batch and wafer, then select a die to read its row, column, coordinates, status, and failure bin. Failed dies belong to the same cluster when edges connect them through dies in the same bin. Use the failure-bin filter to focus the map. The full wafer counts and yield remain visible.
notes: Yield is passing dies divided by tested dies. Tested counts include pass and fail only. Missing and untested sites are reported separately, and locations outside the wafer map are omitted. Cluster links follow shared die edges, so a diagonal touch alone leaves clusters separate.

The measured example uses three MIR-WM811K maps with their original lot, wafer index, and map-level pattern label. Each recorded die reports electrical pass or fail. Row and column restore the source zero-based grid coordinates. The coordinate axes count die pitches from the central grid index and preserve source rows increasing down.

Wafer 20 in lot2 is labeled Center and has 2,145 passing and 315 failing dies, giving 87.20% yield. Its largest edge-connected fail cluster contains 80 dies. Wafer 12 in lot2 is labeled Edge-Loc, and wafer 12 in lot8 is labeled Edge-Ring.

The simulated example uses three generated wafers across two batches. Its illustrative 200 mm outline contains a notch and uses pitches of 10.4 mm horizontally and 11.2 mm vertically. The simulation adds two named failure bins and explicit missing and untested sites.

Simulated wafer A-01 has 234 mapped sites, including 204 pass, 21 fail, five untested, and four missing. The yield is 204 ÷ 225, or 90.67%. The code example uses a small illustrative subset of die states.

lcms-feature-map.summary: Locate detected liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry features by retention time and mass-to-charge ratio, then inspect the recorded scans for a selected mass trace.
lcms-feature-map.useWhen: Use a feature map to investigate overlapping chromatographic signals, distinguish separate mass traces grouped in one feature, and review the scan evidence behind a detection.
lcms-feature-map.data: Supply a unique feature ID, its reported retention time in seconds, mass-to-charge ratio, signal intensity, and any available mass traces. Each trace has its own ID and m/z, a footprint given by retention-time and m/z vertices, and optional scan samples and extraction bounds. A feature without trace data still has its reported position in the overview.
lcms-feature-map.reading: Select an apex marker in the overview or use the Detected feature picker. The overview uses retention time in minutes. The mass-trace panel shows all footprints at their recorded m/z coordinates. Choose an ion trace to inspect its individual footprint in parts per million relative to that trace’s centroid. Use the scan control or select a point on the chromatogram to inspect the nearest recorded scan.
notes: Footprints show the retention-time and m/z extent reported by feature detection. The footprint detail and chromatogram share a retention-time axis in seconds. The shaded strip shows the selected extraction window. The scan readout shows the source ID, time, signal, and the extraction m/z bounds when supplied. Include a charge when the source assigns one.

A zero sample means that the extraction returned zero signal for a recorded scan. A null intensity marks an unavailable value. Keep the source scan IDs and retention times so these two cases remain distinguishable.

Apex marker color represents feature intensity relative to the strongest feature in the supplied map. The logarithmic scale covers four orders of magnitude. Zero signal uses the lightest shade. Use the footprints and assigned charge to review a detection. Confirm compound identity with evidence such as matching MS/MS spectra or a reference standard.

The measured example uses an OpenMS positive-mode teaching run with 334 MS1 scans. OpenMS 3.6.0 detected 75 features with multiple traces using the tutorial’s 10 ppm mass tolerance, 10,000 intensity threshold, and fixed elution-peak width filtering, with trace hull reporting enabled.

For the measured example, feature intensity is the peak area estimated by OpenMS in arbitrary units × seconds. Each chromatogram reading sums measured centroid intensities within ±10 ppm of the selected trace’s centroid m/z in that MS1 scan. The two measures use different units.
The code sample uses illustrative features and scan readings to demonstrate the data structure.

chromatogram-peak-integration.summary: Measure chromatographic peak area between a detector trace and an editable baseline.
chromatogram-peak-integration.useWhen: Review manual integration choices, remeasure a peak after refining its limits, or compare how baseline drift changes the integrated response across peaks.
chromatogram-peak-integration.data: Supply detector readings as [retention time, signal] pairs in strictly increasing time order. Time spacing may vary. Give each peak a unique ID and a start and end within the measured trace. Neighboring windows can touch at an endpoint. Set the time and detector units to match the acquisition.
chromatogram-peak-integration.reading: Select a peak to edit. Drag its time limits and baseline endpoints on the chart, or enter exact values in the numeric fields. The selected region and peak area update together. Reset region restores the supplied settings within the current neighboring boundaries.
notes: The component integrates the original piecewise-linear trace against the straight line between the two baseline endpoints. It interpolates readings at the window limits and inserts an intersection wherever the corrected signal crosses the baseline, then integrates each portion with trapezoids.

Area above baseline includes the positive portions. Signed area adds the negative portions algebraically. Area is expressed in detector response multiplied by the input time unit. The apex marks the largest baseline-corrected response within the window. The trace and its samples are retained through every edit.

Omit a peak’s baseline to connect the interpolated detector readings at the two window endpoints. Supply both endpoint signals to start from a custom baseline. The gallery card displays the integration without editing controls.

The measured example retains all 1,501 readings at 225 nm from 12 to 22 minutes in the first coffee injection published by Guillaume Erny, Marzieh Moeenfard, and Arminda Alves (2021) under CC BY 4.0. Detector response uses the archived scale, so the area is reported in source units × min.

The example uses illustrative windows to examine partially resolved peaks. Its areas quantify the detector response in those windows. Use reference standards to assign compound identities and calibration to estimate concentrations.
The code sample uses simulated readings, including a peak that crosses its baseline near the leading edge. Its first peak has 3 mAU × min above baseline and a signed area of 2.6875 mAU × min.

gauge-rr.summary: Inspect every repeated measurement in a crossed Gauge R&R study and trace the estimated variance to parts, repeatability, operators, and part × operator interaction.
gauge-rr.useWhen: Compare repeated measurements of the same parts across operators. Use the matrix to find where operators differ and the variance breakdown to quantify how much the measuring system contributes in this study.
gauge-rr.data: Supply readings in one measurement unit. Each reading needs a part ID, operator ID, trial ID, and numeric value. Include at least two parts, two operators, and two trials. Supply exactly one reading per trial for every part and operator pair, using the same trial IDs throughout.
gauge-rr.reading: Select a part and operator cell to inspect its original trial values. The absolute view uses a common measurement scale. The part-centered view subtracts each part’s observed mean from every reading for that part. Zero represents that observed mean. This display choice leaves the raw values and the fitted variance components unchanged.
notes: The same operators measure every part. The balanced, crossed random-effects ANOVA retains the part × operator interaction. Repeatability describes variation between trials within a part and operator cell. Reproducibility combines the operator component and the part × operator interaction.

The hierarchy adds variance components in squared measurement units. Total variance is the sum of part-to-part and gauge variance. Gauge variance is the sum of repeatability, operator, and interaction variance. Shares of total variance use the total estimate as denominator. Shares within the gauge use the gauge estimate. An estimate of zero in the denominator leaves that share unavailable.

The variance breakdown uses zero for a component whose method-of-moments estimate is negative and exposes the original estimate for inspection. A zero estimate shows the component was estimated at the boundary.

The baseline and corrected examples use Tables 7 and 9 of Yáñez-Contreras et al. (2026). Each contains 60 measured thread pitch diameters in inches, with ten parts, three appraisers, and two trials. The two studies used different parts on different days with the same appraisers and protocol. The later study estimates a lower absolute gauge standard deviation and a higher gauge share of total variance. Part-to-part variance was also lower in the later set.
The runnable code sample uses simulated measurements in millimeters.

kaplan-meier.summary: Estimate component reliability from failures and right-censored observations. Inspect the specimens and risk set behind each step.
kaplan-meier.useWhen: Compare groups of components observed from a common time origin when some specimens finish follow-up without a recorded failure. Choose cohorts with well-defined test conditions and retain the original censoring times.
kaplan-meier.data: Supply a time unit and at least one cohort with a unique ID and a label. Give every observation a unique ID within its cohort, a finite nonnegative elapsed time, and a status of failed or censored. All specimens enter the risk set at time zero.
kaplan-meier.reading: Choose a cohort and inspect an observation time using the slider or the plot. Each step reports the number at risk immediately before that time, failures and right-censored observations at that time, and the remaining risk set. Use the specimen timeline and event ledger to inspect the underlying records.
notes: The Kaplan–Meier estimate starts at one before any events and multiplies by one minus the ratio of failures to specimens at risk at each failure time. When failures and censoring share a time, both count in the risk set for the failure step. Both are then removed for the next time. Censor-only times leave the estimate unchanged.

A right-censored endpoint records the last observed time for a specimen that had no recorded failure by that time. The at-risk table counts specimens just before each displayed time. Every curve ends at its cohort's last observation.

The chart uses Greenwood variance with a log–log transformation for approximate pointwise 95% confidence bounds where defined. Interpret the estimate and bounds in light of the study design and the assumption that censoring is independent of failure time.

The measured example contains 24 glass capacitors from the 200, 300, and 350 V settings at 170 °C in Zelen’s National Bureau of Standards life test. Each test stand began with eight capacitors. Testing stopped at the fourth failure and the four remaining capacitors were right-censored at that hour. The chart assigns specimen IDs for inspection.
Each voltage setting used one test stand. The curves describe the recorded cohorts under their test conditions.

The runnable example uses illustrative test records. At 120 hours in cohort A, four specimens are at risk, one fails, and one is censored. Survival falls to 75% and two specimens remain at risk immediately afterward.

weibull-probability.summary: Compare time-to-failure observations with a fitted Weibull distribution on probability paper. Inspect early departures and fitted lifetime percentiles.
weibull-probability.useWhen: Compare groups such as manufacturing lots, suppliers, or test conditions when each specimen has a recorded failure time or a right-censoring time. Keep the groups and test conditions visible when interpreting their fits.
weibull-probability.data: Supply a shared elapsed time unit and cohorts with unique IDs and labels. Each specimen needs an ID unique within its cohort, a finite positive elapsed time, and a status of failed or censored. All specimens enter at time zero.
weibull-probability.reading: The horizontal axis shows time on a logarithmic scale. The vertical axis spaces cumulative failure percentages according to ln(−ln(1−p)), so a fitted two-parameter Weibull appears as a straight line. Select a failure to compare its observed time with the fitted time at the same plotted probability. Choose a fitted percentile to compare model lifetimes across cohorts.
notes: Observed failures are placed halfway up each Kaplan–Meier failure step on the cumulative failure scale. Tied failures share one plotting probability, with all specimens still at risk included in that step. Right-censored observations appear below the probability axis at their last observed times.

The two-parameter fit uses maximum likelihood independently of the plotting positions. Failure times contribute through the Weibull density. Right-censored times contribute the probability of surviving to that time. A cohort whose observations cannot identify a finite fit has no fitted line.

The selected failure’s horizontal span ends at its fitted time at the same probability. The ratio divides observed elapsed time by fitted elapsed time. A ratio below one indicates an earlier failure than the fitted quantile.

B10 and B50 are the fitted times by which 10% and 50% of the cohort would have failed under the model. Fit segments outside the cohort’s observed time range represent extrapolation. Read the fitted percentiles in light of the sample size and the recorded test conditions.

The measured example preserves all 63 recorded failure times in seconds from Bhaumik, Kumar, and Bharathwaj’s four-ball rolling contact fatigue tests on AISI 52100 bearing steel. Each calcium grease grade, EP0, EP00, and EP000, has 21 failures. The fixture uses version 3 of the dataset under CC BY 4.0.

The supplier example uses simulated test records in hours. Each illustrative supplier has eight failures and four right-censored observations at a 1,600-hour cutoff. Supplier A includes an early failure at 180 hours and a failure tied with the cutoff censors.
The runnable example uses smaller simulated supplier cohorts and includes both failures and right-censored observations.

hotelling-process-monitor.summary: Monitor joint changes in process measurements against a fixed reference. Select a run to inspect its channel measurements, covariance geometry, and signed contributions to Hotelling T².
hotelling-process-monitor.useWhen: Track successive runs with several correlated measurements per run, such as spindle current, vibration, and acoustic emission from machining passes. Establish a reference period under stable process conditions before monitoring new runs.
hotelling-process-monitor.data: Define at least two channels with unique IDs. Supply a finite measurement per channel in every observation, using a consistent channel order and units. Provide more reference observations than channels and a full-rank reference covariance. Include at least one monitoring run, place runs in acquisition order, and use unique observation IDs within each group.
hotelling-process-monitor.reading: Each plotted run has a Hotelling T² score and an upper control limit. Select a run to see where two of its standardized measurements fall inside or outside the projected boundary. Change the axis pair to inspect other channels. The signed contribution plot shows every channel’s term in the selected run’s total T².
notes: The reference fixes the sample means and covariance. Each new run’s T² is its squared Mahalanobis distance from the reference mean. Covariance matters because a combination of otherwise ordinary readings can depart from the relationships established in the reference.

The one-sided Phase II limit uses p(m + 1)(m − 1) / [m(m − p)] times the (1 − α) quantile of the F distribution with p and m − p degrees of freedom. Here p is the channel count and m is the reference sample count. The nominal per-run false alarm probability α assumes independent observations from the same multivariate normal process in the reference and follow-up. Treat consecutive exceedances or non-normal data in light of the sampling design.
When the score axis shows log₁₊, vertical positions use log(1 + T²) and the tick labels show T². This keeps the lower scores legible when the follow-up includes extreme values.

The ellipse is the projection of the full control region onto the displayed pair of standardized channels. A point outside it exceeds the full limit. With additional channels, an inside point can still exceed the full limit. Read each run’s alert from the full-channel score.

For standardized readings z and reference correlation matrix R, channel j contributes zⱼ × (R⁻¹z)ⱼ. The signed contributions sum to T². A negative value offsets positive terms through the fitted correlations. Use these terms to prioritize review while investigating physical causes independently.

The measured example uses Milling Wear Case 11 from UC Berkeley’s BEST Lab, published by NASA. The test recorded 23 passes on cast iron at 0.75 mm cutting depth and 0.25 mm per revolution. Each channel is the mean of samples 1,801–7,200 from its 9,000-sample pass. The channels retain their recorded scales. The vibration and acoustic emission channels are recorded envelopes from the test hardware.

The example retrospectively fixes the reference at passes 01–08 and monitors passes 09–23 at α = 0.01. Pass 15 is the first exceedance, at T² = 64.27 against a limit of 56.98. Eight follow-up runs exceed the limit. This split illustrates the method on an ordered wear test. The limit is a model-based reference for that sequence.

At Pass 15, table acoustic emission contributes 64.25 to T². The current and vibration terms nearly cancel. Select current and vibration as the displayed axes to see this run inside their projected boundary with its full-channel alert still active.
The runnable example uses simulated shaft diameter, spindle load, and motor current.

classifier-threshold-explorer.summary: Explore how a binary classifier trades missed failures against false alarms. One threshold links the operating points on the ROC and precision–recall curves with the counts in the confusion matrix.
classifier-threshold-explorer.useWhen: Review scored inspection results with known outcomes. Compare the burden of sending passing items for review with the benefit of catching more failures.
classifier-threshold-explorer.data: Supply one record per evaluated item with a unique ID, a finite score and its observed outcome. Higher scores must indicate stronger evidence for the positive class. Include both observed classes and give each a descriptive label.
classifier-threshold-explorer.reading: Move the threshold slider or pick a plotted operating point. The ROC marker shows recall versus the false-positive rate, while the precision–recall marker shows how many flagged items actually failed. The confusion matrix shows observed outcomes in rows and threshold predictions in columns.
notes: A score at or above the threshold predicts the positive class. All items with identical scores change classification together. Each observed score is one threshold stop, and an additional stop above the highest score predicts every item as negative.

Recall divides caught failures by all observed failures. The false-positive rate divides false alarms by all observed passes. Precision divides caught failures by all items flagged at the current threshold. Precision is undefined when no items are flagged.

ROC AUC uses trapezoidal area between attainable points. Average precision weights precision at each score group by its increase in recall. The precision–recall plot uses steps that reflect this weighting. The horizontal line shows the positive fraction in the evaluated sample.

The SECOM example uses observed semiconductor line-test outcomes from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. A class-balanced L2 logistic model (C = 0.01) was fitted on 1,208 July–September 2008 records, including 82 failures. The preprocessing dropped constant and entirely missing features, then fitted median imputation and standardization using those training records.

The final October 2008 block contains 359 held-out tests with 22 failures. Its observed positive rate is 6.13%. The displayed scores rank failures for threshold inspection. They are model outputs on this retrospective split. Evaluate calibration and any chosen threshold separately on fresh data before production use.
The runnable example uses synthetic inspection scores for 12 items. Two items share the initial cutoff score of 0.72 and enter the predicted positive class together.

fault-event-replay.useWhen: Reconstruct the order of a process disturbance. Inspect which alarms were active, what changed in the equipment, and which measurements were available when an operator acted.
fault-event-replay.data: Supply a start and end time in seconds on a common clock. Give each signal a unique ID, a label, optional units and samples with distinct timestamps. Supply nonoverlapping equipment-state intervals, alarm intervals that may overlap, and timestamped operator actions. Use source records for logged events and describe how you derived any phases.
fault-event-replay.reading: Press Play to advance the cursor at the selected speed or use the scrubber to inspect a recorded sample or event time. Jump to an event from the chronology or use the previous and next event controls. Scrubbing or jumping pauses playback. At each position, inspect the most recent sensor samples, current state, and active alarms.
notes: Each signal uses its last sample at or before the cursor. A missing value or an expired sample leaves the reading unavailable until a valid one arrives. Set maxAge in seconds to specify how long a sample remains current. The plotted trace breaks across gaps.
A state or alarm starts at its start time and clears at its end time. An omitted end leaves it active through the replay window. At an exact boundary the new interval applies.
Keep separate records when alarms, state changes, and operator actions share a timestamp. Shared time aligns the records without establishing causation.

The measured example replays Cranfield Test 3 from the PRONTO multiphase flow benchmark, an induced restriction test on 7 September 2017. It covers 14:47 to 15:57 on the recorded site clock. It shows PT312 air delivery pressure, the FIC302 inlet air flow reading, and the controller output.

The example reconstructs one-second measurement times from acquisition order within each logged minute and retains every fifth row. Valve-opening states and manual changes come from the independent operation log at minute resolution. Instrument-health alarms come from the SCADA alarm log at its recorded precision.
Each valve phase places a manual position change at its logged minute boundary. Inspect the signal response and alarm history around the change, allowing for the operation log’s coarser timing.

The runnable code example uses synthetic pump readings, equipment states, alarms, and operator actions. It includes separate signal sampling times, a pressure data gap, and actions that share timestamps with equipment-state changes.

startup-overlay.summary: Align repeated startups to a recorded event and compare the signals that precede readiness.
startup-overlay.useWhen: Investigate variation in the time it takes equipment to become ready. Compare the pressure, temperature, or load traces of early and late runs, and inspect individual runs for unusual behavior.
startup-overlay.data: Supply a common window relative to startup, a grid step, and an elapsed-time deadline, all in seconds. Assign each run an event timestamp on its own clock. Include time-stamped signals and the last observed time. Supply the first documented readiness timestamp or an explicit failure record when available.
startup-overlay.reading: The zero line is the recorded start in each run. Select a run to compare its signals with the groups. Move the readiness deadline to recalculate the groups and see which runs become late, remain unready, or have insufficient follow-up.
notes: Each run is shifted by its own eventTime. Negative elapsed time shows measurements made before that event when present. Choose the same operational event to anchor each run.

On the common grid, a signal can be interpolated between adjacent measurements within its maxGap, which defaults to twice the grid step. A missing sample breaks the trace. Values beyond the recorded samples remain unavailable.

The cohort line is the median, and the ribbon spans the 25th to 75th percentiles of available runs at each elapsed time. Because coverage can vary over the window, the set of runs contributing to the ribbon can change over time.

A run that reaches readiness by the deadline is on time, including at the deadline itself. A recorded readiness time after it is late. A run with no readiness record and observations through the deadline is not ready by that time. A run whose observations ended earlier has insufficient follow-up at that deadline.
Mark a failure only when the source reports one. Moving the deadline changes the comparison groups while preserving the recorded readiness and failure outcomes.

The measured example uses all 30 laboratory runs at operating points 001–003 for the 1-butanol, 2-propanol, and water mixture. Starting Operation pressure is close to 500 mbar across the runs. Other operating settings can vary. The signals are T703 reboiler liquid temperature and T705 column-top fluid temperature, both in °C.

Elapsed time starts at the first recorded Startup sample. Readiness is the first recorded Operation sample. The comparison uses a 30-second grid and up to five minutes of Operation readings per run, within a 100-minute window. The source clock gap in operating point 001, test 011 is retained.

All 30 runs enter Operation, 1,640 to 5,783 seconds after the first Startup sample. At the illustrative 45-minute deadline, 16 enter Operation on time and 14 enter later. These groups describe startup duration.

The runnable pump example uses synthetic signals and status records. It includes a run ready exactly at 12 seconds, a documented failure, one run with insufficient follow-up, and a missing pressure sample.
