cumulative-flow.summary: Reconstruct jobs in progress at each stage from timestamped job transitions, and inspect the orders behind a growing band.
cumulative-flow.useWhen: Review how concurrent jobs advance through production. Locate stages where work accumulates, then inspect the individual jobs and how long they have been in that stage.
cumulative-flow.data: Supply the window start and end in seconds on a common clock, a list of uniquely identified stages in process order, and timestamped job transitions. Set stage to the destination stage ID, or to null for confirmed completion. Pass opening jobs separately with their original stage entry times.
cumulative-flow.reading: The highest boundary counts all jobs admitted by that time, including opening work in progress. The bottom band counts completed jobs. The active stage bands appear above completion in reverse process order, so the earliest stage sits at the top. The thickness of a stage band gives its job count. Select a time and stage to inspect its entries, exits, and current jobs, ordered by earliest stage entry.
notes: Counts change in steps at recorded events. Events that share a timestamp are applied in input order, and the chart shows the state after the whole group. A visit includes its entry time and ends just before its exit time.

The first transition for a new job records its admission. A transfer exits the previous stage and enters the next one. Rework creates a new visit and adds to the stage entry and exit totals. An explicit null transition closes the job. With no completion event, the job stays in its current stage through the end of the window.

Opening jobs count toward admitted and active totals. Their existing stage entries occurred at or before the start and are supplied in the opening inventory. The entry and exit counters track transitions during the observation window. The sum of active jobs and completed jobs equals admitted jobs at each step.

Use individual job timestamps for dwell and lead time, especially when jobs follow different routes or change order. A widening band shows accumulation. Use the operating records to investigate its cause.

The measured example uses the cleaned process log from a physical smart factory in Trier. It retains 21 successfully stored jobs released from 14:24 to 15:46 on 25 June 2021. The nine omitted jobs lack a successful final storage completion, and some also lack earlier boundaries. The 126 retained boundaries cover the selected cohort through its final successful store at 15:54:20.660 on the source clock.

The storage unload queue spans the recorded unload scheduling and start events. Preparation and transfer spans unload start to oven start. Oven treatment uses the oven start and completion events. Finishing and transfer spans oven completion to scheduled inspection, and inspection and storage ends at the successful store. The grouped stages describe elapsed residence between log boundaries and can include work, transport, and waiting.

At the initial cursor about 9.7 seconds into the window, six of seven admitted jobs in the measured cohort are waiting to unload. The runnable machining example uses simulated records with opening work in progress, a return from inspection to machining, and a job still waiting at the end.

takt-balance.summary: Compare workstation task loads with takt time and test reassignments that preserve task order.
takt-balance.useWhen: Review how work is distributed across a paced line. Find stations over the target and test whether a task can move to relieve an overloaded station.
takt-balance.data: Supply net production time in seconds and required units for the same planning period. List the stations in process order, and give each task a duration per unit and an initial station. Add known task dependencies and station restrictions where applicable.
takt-balance.reading: Each stack shows the work assigned to one station for one unit. The reference line marks takt, the available production seconds divided by demand. Select a task in the chart or the task list, then choose a permitted destination. The stacks and station margins update together. Reset restores the original assignment.
notes: Use net available production time after planned breaks or stops. For 2,520 available seconds and demand of 60 units, takt is 42 seconds per unit.
A station at takt meets the target. Above it, the gap is a time deficit. Below it, the gap is spare time under the supplied workload assumptions.

Predecessors can share a station with a task or be at an earlier station. Tasks at the same station are ordered by their precedence relationships. A capability restriction limits a task to its allowed stations. Moves can create a time deficit so the effect stays visible.

The view adds task times within each station for a single unit. The margins are planning comparisons under the supplied assignments and durations. Actual throughput also depends on factors such as task variability, changeovers, blocking, and simultaneous work.

The automotive example uses normalized pre-automation times from the published Yamazumi worksheet for three operators. It groups the listed times into 15 work elements. The workbook lists an 11.4-second total for Operator 3. Its listed elements sum to 11.2 seconds, which the chart uses as the initial load.

The comparison assumes 37,800 net production seconds for 3,600 units, giving a takt of 10.5 seconds per unit. The recorded element times give initial loads of 9.5, 10.2, and 11.2 seconds. Moving the 1-second Process 13 from Operator 3 to Operator 1 gives 10.5, 10.2, and 10.2 seconds.

The scenario keeps walking and support work with their source operators. Routine work can move between operators at unchanged task times in the scenario. The workbook records anonymized work elements and their times.

The runnable enclosure example uses simulated data. Preparation starts at 45 seconds, Assembly at 25, and Verification at 21. Moving Deburr holes to Assembly leaves 28, 42, and 21 seconds. Moving it to Verification would put it after seating the inserts.

process-control.summary: Review successive measurements against a process baseline and compare their distribution with specified bounds.
process-control.useWhen: Show an individuals control chart to inspect stability over observation order. Show a capability histogram to compare the distribution with engineering specifications.
process-control.data: For the individuals chart, pass ordered observations and a series of readings to TimeSeries, with precomputed control limits and rule markers in spcTracks. For the histogram, pass ordered bin edges and counts to Distribution, with optional specification and target markers.
process-control.reading: The individuals chart compares each measurement with a center line and control limits estimated from a baseline. The histogram shows counts per bin and how the readings sit relative to specification limits.
notes: The examples use 195 heat flow meter calibration factors collected by NIST. The source gives the observation order and leaves the calibration factor unit unspecified.

The individuals example fixes its center and control limits from the first 100 readings. Limits are the baseline mean plus or minus three times the mean moving range divided by 1.128. Observation 189 falls below the lower control limit in the follow-up portion.

The histogram counts the readings in 14 bins of width 0.01. It shows illustrative specification limits of 9.20 and 9.32 and a target of 9.26. Use approved engineering specifications and assess stability before calculating process capability.
